Effects on the eyes. When a diabetic patient who had experi- enced bilateral visual loss for several months and who had been taking chlorpropamide for one year stopped treatment, visual acuity improved and colour vision rapidly returned.1 A 5-day challenge with chlorpropamide resulted in a mild decrease in acuity followed by return to baseline values when treatment was again stopped. Drug-induced optic neuropathy was considered to have occurred. There is also a report of a patient with type 2 dia- betes mellitus who developed myopia two days after starting treatment with glibenclamide 10 mg daily.2 Visual difficulties re- solved a few days after stopping glibenclamide. 1. Wymore J, Carter JE. Chlorpropamide-induced optic neuropa- thy. Arch Intern Med 1982; 142: 381. 2. Teller J, et al. Accommodation insufficiency induced by glyben- clamide. Ann Ophthalmol 1989; 21: 275–6. Effects on the kidneys. The nephrotic syndrome has been re- ported in a patient treated with chlorpropamide.1 Serological testing and renal biopsy showed that the glomerular lesions were of an immune-complex nature. Both the nephrotic syndrome and the glomerulonephritis resolved after treatment was stopped. The patient also developed a skin eruption, hepatitis, and eosino- philia. 1. Appel GB, et al. Nephrotic syndrome and immune complex glomerulonephritis associated with chlorpropamide therapy. Am J Med 1983; 74: 337–42. Effects on the liver. Chlorpropamide was implicated1 in 8 of 53 cases of drug-induced acute liver disease admitted to a hospi- tal in Jamaica over the years 1973 to 1988. Hepatocanalicular cholestasis occurred in 5 cases and diffuse necrosis in 3. One pa- tient with massive hepatic necrosis died. Intrahepatic cholesta- sis,2-4 an acute hepatitis-like syndrome,5 and a combination of both6 have been described in patients receiving glibenclamide. 1. Lee MG, et al.
